title: Architecture Standards: API, Coding, Infra, Model-Serving, Observability, Performance, and ADRs
author: Priya Raman
body:
Summary
-------
This document consolidates Redwood Inference's architecture standards across API design, coding practices, infrastructure, model-serving, observability, performance targets, and the ADR (Architecture Decision Record) process. It establishes required defaults, concrete SLO targets, and required review/rollout steps for changes that affect production inference behavior.

Scope
-----
Applies to all services and teams that develop production inference endpoints, control plane services, platform tooling, and customer-facing APIs. Exceptions must be recorded in an ADR and approved by the owning service lead and platform architecture.

Principles
----------
- Developer-first: APIs and infra should be easy to adopt and maintainable for engineers.
- Production-first: defaults favor reliability, observability, and clear SLAs.
- Measurable: every standard includes metrics and thresholds.
- Incremental change: breaking changes require ADR + migration plan + deprecation window.

1) API Standards
----------------
Purpose: ensure consistent, predictable, and secure APIs across Redwood products (hosted, dedicated, private deployments).

Design and contract
- Use REST/JSON for public HTTP APIs; gRPC allowed for internal high-throughput control-plane services.
- All public endpoints must have OpenAPI (v3) spec checked into the service repo under /api/openapi.yaml.
- API versioning: major version in path (e.g. /v1/...), minor compatibility changes via header X-Redwood-API-Version if necessary.
- Use consistent resource naming: kebab-case for endpoints and snake_case for JSON properties.

Error handling and idempotency
- Return structured errors: {"code": "string", "message": "string", "request_id": "uuid"}.
- Use standard HTTP codes: 400 (client), 401/403 (auth), 429 (rate limit), 5xx (server).
- Long-running operations: expose operation resources (POST -> 202 with Location header).
- Clients must be able to retry idempotent operations; design endpoints with idempotency keys when side-effects occur.

Rate limiting and throttling
- Token-based rate limiting per account with tier defaults: free/dev: 60 req/min, standard: 600 req/min, enterprise: configurable.
- Endpoints that produce streaming token output have separate concurrency and token-rate limits.

API example (OpenAPI snippet)
```yaml
paths:
  /v1/generate:
    post:
      summary: Generate text
      responses:
        '200':
          description: successful response
```

2) Coding Standards
--------------------
Purpose: consistency, security, and maintainability across Redwood codebases.

Languages and repositories
- Primary backend languages: Go (control plane), Rust/C++ (core runtime), Python (SDKs, evals).
- Monorepo allowed for related teams; microrepos acceptable with dependency and CI requirements.

Static checks and testing
- Every PR must pass: linting, type checks (where applicable), unit tests, and integration smoke tests.
- Minimum test coverage policy: service-level 60% (aim for >80% for core infra).
- Security SCA scans run in CI; fix high-critical findings before merge.

PR and review process
- Use feature branches, descriptive titles, and link relevant ADRs or tickets.
- Require at least one reviewer from owning team and one from platform for infra-impacting changes.

Style and patterns
- Follow language-specific style guides (golangci-lint config, rustfmt, black/flake8).
- Prefer explicit dependency versions and reproducible builds.

3) Infrastructure Standards
--------------------------
Purpose: safe, auditable, and scalable infra for hosted and private deployments.

IaC and provisioning
- Terraform is the canonical IaC tool. Modules must live in terraform-modules/* and be reviewed through platform team.
- All changes to production infra require a plan reviewed and approved by platform + security.

Networking and zones
- All public-facing services must be deployed across a minimum of 2 AZs per region.
- Private deployments: provide default VPC templates and clear docs for customer-provided networking.

Secrets and key management
- Use KMS/HSM for all production encryption keys. Secrets stored in a secrets manager (Vault/Secrets Manager) and never in plaintext in repos.

Cost and capacity controls
- Each team must own monthly spend dashboard and alert if 7-day burn rate exceeds forecasted by >20%.

4) Model-Serving Standards
--------------------------
Purpose: ensure models are packaged, versioned, and served with predictable performance and safe defaults.

Model packaging and artifacts
- Model artifacts must include: model weights, tokenizer, config (model card), quantization profile (if applied), and a small-suite of regression prompts in /evals/regression/*.
- Acceptable artifact formats: TorchScript, ONNX, or vendor-provided formats. Include a small adapter if using a custom runtime.

Versioning and compatibility
- Model versions use semver-like labels: model-name@vMAJOR.MINOR (e.g., redwood-llama-8b@v1.2).
- Backwards-compatible tokenizer/config changes increment minor; weight/architecture changes increment major and require ADR.

Serving configurations
- Default serving profile for a model must include: max_batch_size, max_concurrency, sequence_length_limit, kv_cache_policy. Submit profile as model-name.json in model registry.
- Quantization: allowed with documented quality tests. Quantization profiles are stored and tagged with accuracy/regression scores.

Safety and quality
- Every model onboarded to production must pass the model-evals regression suite with no priority-regression failures. Failing prompts must have triage notes in regression-triage/ with owner and remediation plan.

KV cache and caching policies
- Prefix caching allowed for recurring prompts; cache keys must be keyed by model_version + prompt_hash + relevant parameters. Time-to-live defaults: 6 hours for generated outputs unless explicitly shorter.

5) Observability Standards
--------------------------
Purpose: ensure consistent telemetry for debugging, SLO monitoring, and cost/efficiency analysis.

Metrics
- Use Prometheus exposition format and standard metric names with labels. Required metrics for inference endpoints: request_count, request_latency_ms (histogram), tokens_generated, kv_cache_hit_ratio, model_load_time_ms, error_count.
- Label conventions: service, route, model_name, model_version, region, environment.

Tracing and logs
- Distributed tracing via OpenTelemetry; spans should include model_name, model_version, request_id, and sampling priority.
- Structured JSON logs with level, message, request_id, latency_ms, and error details. PII must be redacted at ingestion.

Dashboards and SLOs
- Create per-service dashboards showing P50/P95/P99 latency, error rate, token throughput, and cost per token.
- SLOs must be defined and have owner and burn-rate alerts (see Performance section).

6) Performance Standards and SLO Targets
---------------------------------------
Purpose: define measurable performance SLOs and testing requirements for production inference. Targets are baseline defaults; teams must justify deviations in an ADR.

Service class SLOs (examples)
| Model class | P50 latency (per-token) | P95 latency | P99 latency | availability (monthly SLA) |
|-------------|-------------------------:|------------:|------------:|--------------------------:|
| Tiny (< 1B) | 10ms                    | 40ms        | 150ms       | 99.95%                   |
| Small (1B-8B)| 20ms                   | 100ms       | 400ms       | 99.9%                    |
| Large (8B-70B)| 50ms                  | 300ms       | 800ms       | 99.9%                    |

Notes:
- Per-token latency depends on runtime and hardware; the numbers above are targets for hosted-prod on dedicated class GPUs. Private deployments must specify expected SLOs in the customer agreement.
- Availability measured by successful request completion (non-5xx) over rolling 30d windows.

Load and performance testing
- Every service must include a perf suite in benchmarking-and-perf-suite/ that can reproduce steady-state QPS and spike tests.
- Run load tests for major releases and before capacity increases. Document test harness, dataset, and environment used.

Cost-performance controls
- Default autoscaling policies should favor maintaining P95 latency under SLO while minimizing overprovisioning. Use batching and prefix caching before allocating more GPUs when possible.

7) ADR (Architecture Decision Record) Process
-------------------------------------------
Purpose: formalize decisions that change the architecture or standards.

When to open an ADR
- Any change that affects cross-team contracts, API shapes, model packaging or serving defaults, infra assumptions, or SLO targets.

ADR template (required fields)
- Title
- Date
- Status: proposed | accepted | deprecated
- Context and problem statement
- Considered alternatives
- Decision and rationale
- Consequences and migration plan
- Owners and reviewers

Lifecycle and storage
- Store ADRs under architecture-and-standards/adrs/ with short descriptive filenames (e.g., adr-model-versioning-2026-02-01.md).
- ADRs must be reviewed by platform architecture and the affected service owners. Accepted ADRs should be referenced in the relevant standards sections and implementation repos.

Example ADR summary
- adr-model-versioning-2025-11-02: Adopted semver-like model versioning and model registry metadata requirements (owners: runtime-team, platform). Consequence: added model compat checks to CI and an automated migration tool for tokenizer changes.

Change / rollout checklist (required for infra, API, serving, or SLO changes)
1. Open ADR describing intent and migration strategy.
2. Add tests (unit, integration, perf) and CI gating.
3. Stakeholder review: platform, security (if infra), customer-success (if customer-visible), and product.
4. Gradual rollout plan: canary (1%), regional rollout, global.
5. Monitoring: pre/post metrics baseline and rollout dashboards.
6. Rollback and postmortem plan.

Ownership and governance
- Platform Architecture team maintains this document. Service owners are responsible for keeping their service-specific configurations in compliance. Quarterly reviews of standards take place and require sign-off to update.

Appendices
---------
A. Standard metric names
- redwood_inference_request_count_total
- redwood_inference_request_latency_ms_bucket
- redwood_inference_tokens_generated_total

B. Example CI gate command for perf smoke test
```bash
# run benchmark harness against staging
bin/run-bench --config staging.yaml --target qps=100 --duration=300s
```
